- Our research is concentrated on examining the presentation and diagnostic assessment of chronic myocarditis, a disease known for its complexity in identification and management. - Due to the unavailability of unique biomarkers for myocarditis, the assessment of electrocardiogram (ECG) results has become increasingly important in establishing the diagnosis, especially in those with suspected acute myocarditis. - Our initial findings indicate that individuals with acute myocarditis can experience quick deterioration in cardiac abnormalities, which may include coronary artery involvement and significant ventricular dysfunction, detectable through ECG and other imaging modalities. - Although fulminant myocarditis has been linked to poor outcomes, there are limited data regarding the long-term development and prognosis of chronic myocarditis, especially in those with persistent ventricular dysfunction despite adequate treatment. - This research aims to uncover clinical and laboratory indicators that may provide crucial insights into the underlying pathophysiology and management of chronic myocarditis, highlighting early predictors of disease progression and response to treatment. - Our results demonstrate that myocarditis is a multifaceted and diverse ailment, manifesting in various clinical presentations and outcomes depending on the underlying cause and severity of myocardial inflammation.

Our investigation of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) involved an in-depth exploration of the malignant mutations in the myosin gene that may be the root cause of this disease. We utilized microarray technology to study the expression patterns of several regulatory genes in the affected hearts. We uncovered a broad spectrum of expression levels among these genes, with a notable contrast between two particular gene clusters. To test our hypothesis, we formulated an intervention plan based on the application of a mixture of amino acids, including arginine, to transgenic mice with altered myosin genes. Subsequently, we observed a significant decrease in the expression levels of HCM-causing genes in these mice. Based on these findings, we posit that arginine-based dietary interventions could have promising implications for the treatment of HCM. Our observations were further substantiated by the analysis of bioinformatics data using the HGTI and LCR databases.
